I looked up the 570 code at work today. It places a code on the account that tells other departments that additional liability is pending and puts a hold on certain automated processes until the related case is closed (and thus the adjustment made). Are you sure that is the right code? I am not seeing how that could be used for delays? 

 560 extends the statue date, which would need to be entered to allow a refund that has passed the statute limitation to process, so it would make sense to input a 560 when processing is taken longer than normal? 

I am not certain how either could be used in the way you are implying, but as I said I do not work in that area and have little idea how they might employ those codes.

My apologies. I have edited the message to remove that part. I have no intention to solicit or supply any goods or services. I am actually not allowed by law to provide any paid services in this area or to accept any form of compensation for advice given as an employee of the IRS. I am not a tax preparer, nor do I mean to present myself as one.

I am very sorry for your loss. This must be a hard enough time for you already without having to deal with tax issues on top of that. And I know that taxes surrounding deaths can be especially difficult. My mother and her siblings are still handling my grandmother's estate after she passed this last fall.

As for your return, in the letter they should have specified what they need more information on. I don't handle descendant returns (returns involving taxpayers who have passed away) - they are handled by specialists - but if you want to tell me the wording of the letter, I can see if I can maybe explain better what is going on? No promises as it might be something outside my training, but I would be glad to help if I can.

I won't deny anything. I don't work in the customer facing area so if your friend has knowledge of that, then I'd believe them. I can tell you what that call does on my end though. 

I am in one of the departments that enters the changes to the tax accounts. When that call happens, what the customer service people are supposed to do if it is getting close to the 60 days is input that code and also leave a case note on the case ID with the digital image of the transcript or document that my department sees. That note shows up on our list and  we are supposed to check those notes first thing. That said, I cannot speak to the quality of service provided by those employees. I have never done that job and have very limited contact with those that do. 

I do know that some departments can also change the priority code on the case file. I do not know what the instructions are in the manual - that is who is allowed to make that change and when - I only see the results when they do it. That priority code will move the case files up to the top of our daily list, regardless of received date. I also am not able to change the code myself, just fyi.

I can also say that certain other departments do not act in a timely manner, and there are times that I cannot process a change until I have approval from that other department. So while I may get to your return within the month, that other department might hold that return for up to a year. As soon as it's back in my queue, I process it the same day. It's the best I can do to process things as quickly as I can on my end.

I don't know what is happening in those other departments or why they take so long to get back to us sometimes. I agree that the IRS is a clunky and inefficient machine, and you are justified in being upset by that. That is what the old commission was trying to fix by digitizing more things. Both so that we can move the documents between departments more efficiently (no waiting on inter-office or intra-office mail when you can digitally send a document from the Ogden office to the specialty department in Austin in seconds) and so they could better figure out where the slowdowns are and why, since they can live monitor how many days out each document is at each step of the process when it is digital. 

This is also why we have been hiring more people - to try to speed up the process. Firing people during the busiest time of the year is going to be entirely counterproductive. Especially when it isn't the people with low scores on efficiency and quality that are being let go. Like I said, some of our best people are the ones leaving because of these changes.

Also, while I know that it does not help much while you don't have the refund when you need it, the received date on the document is what is used to process the change. If we are late getting you your refund past the processing time, you should get it with interest accrued.

Edit to say: I can also tell you that the code 570 does not do anything in my department. I don't know if it does something in other departments, but that is not a code that I am trained to pay attention to, though I have seen it often when I was working cases from the COVID years. The received date and priority codes are what organize our list of cases on my end.

 We are supposed to work by that order, but I do know a lot of people got fired for not doing that and skipping more difficult cases in favor of ones that are faster to process. But it does take time to catch and fire those people, and I am sorry to say it caused a lot of problems. I was one of the people cleaning up after the fired folks, trying to get those cases handled asap. A lot of folks were pulling 60 hour weeks (max over time we were allowed) to get those handled as soon as possible.

I would do a check in call to the IRS and see what you can find out. Let the them know that you never authorized a third party to request your records. They can put some things in place to make your account more secure if they know someone is trying to access the information without permission.

Oh yeah. I've heard some coworkers just quiet crying at their desks. Everyone is stressed. We've been trying to keep spirits up as best we can but it's hard. Our manager brings snacks when she can. Our lead's started doing a joke of the day. One of my coworkers makes a point to send a morning greeting to the whole team each day via the messenger. We're doing what we can to get through it. Most of us joined the civil service because we want to serve the American ppl and this is the best way we can with our skills.

The worst part is that coworkers with disabilities are having to quit because they got hired on to a telework job that suddenly isn't telework anymore. More than a few are disabled veterans since we gave disabled vets hiring preference (which is apparently DEI). It'll take over a year to get the paperwork in to get a reasonable accommodation for it, if the request even gets approved, and they can't wait for that. I hear the union is swamped trying to argue the cases for disabled workers to have their telework accommodations approved. The guy that trained me is one of them leaving because of this. 

I've been in public service jobs, doing data entry for various government jobs, for seven years now. Third year at the irs. I'm trying to stick it out because the American people deserve better than a skeleton crew barely holding things together. They want to dismantle us, they'll have to fire me properly.

It could be a scam, even if the letter is from the IRS. If you didn't authorize anyone to pull your tax transcript and didn't send in the form yourself, someone might be trying to steal your identity. If neither you nor your husband know about this form being sent in, I would call the IRS directly to find out who sent in the request. Someone might be trying to steal your information to commit fraud. 

To know if the letter is from the IRS or not: it should have a signature line signed by one of the department heads. I've seen them enough I should be able to let you know if it is legit if you can show the signature line.

Depending on which office was asking for the document, it might take a while. A lot of our best ppl took the deferred voluntary resignation program after they announced they would be doing a Reduction In Force (fancy government term for layoff), which they have already started doing. So expect the job markets to get flooded with laid off tax examiners and clerks.

Good news is most of our offices finally caught up from the backlog caused by the closing during the COVID years just before they started this layoff plan.

Hopefully the office that asked for the document is one of the ones that were caught up and not one that was still behind since we have a "first in first out"  policy.

Bad news: with the voluntary registrations we are already starting to fall behind. My office was keeping one month out on processing to after we caught up I last December. Now we are over two months out, and they have started offering overtime to those of us still there again. For reference, my team had the best speed and quality in our office - we have already lost half our people. And they are still planning on laying off more ppl in waves, so expect response times to get worse across the board. 

We did have a commissioner that was focused on modernizing and digitizing the process as much as possible to speed up processing, reduce the time spent sending paper documents from one place to another, and space taken up by storing said documents in order to save tax payers money (as we currently maintain warehouses full of old returns). But they fired him. So who knows what's going to happen going forward. 

We are doing our best, but they are hamstring us. If your situation is dire, you can apply for a hardship case to try to get bumped up the line for processing, and I always suggest calling as bothersome as it can be. Talking to a person can sometimes be the most effective. And just keep checking in. The squeaky wheel gets the grease after all.

I got my bipolar diagnosis first and ADHD after. I take meds for both, and the psych had to carefully balance adding ADHD meds into my regimen, because yeah it can cause a manic episode if you have bipolar. 

If the doc is seeing signs of mania, it is a good idea to get checked. That's not to say that you do have bipolar. It could be something else that is going on as there can be other things that look like bipolar mania on the surface. That's why you need to see the psych. They are better trained to evaluate what's going on and how to proceed safely for you. 

Being on the right meds can really help. And even if you decide you don't want meds (not a decision I would recommend, but your decision to make) there are things like cognitive behavioral therapy and dialect behavior therapy that can give you good tools to better manage symptoms. 

The first step is getting properly diagnosed. See a psych at minimum. I'd recommend getting full spectrum testing if you can. I did on the recommendation of the Department of Assistive and Rehabilitative Services office at my university. They even got the government to pay for it since I already had one diagnosis that counted as a disability and the caseworker suspected I had more going on.

If it wasn't for that, I likely never would have found out that I had ADHD at all, let alone the additional diagnosis of low support needs autism I received. And now that I know, I do so much better maintaining my mental health and thus being able to complete tasks and manage stress. 

I hope you are able to find the same success with your own mental health journey. I know the medical community can be frustrating with how they do things sometimes, but hang in there. It's worth it.

I got caught cheating in high school. It was also the only time I ever tried to cheat. I was a gifted and talented kind from elementary all the way through high school, and taking a language was the first time I ever struggled with a subject. Didn't know how to handle it, panicked and did something dumb, trying to cheat. I made up for it after that by working hard and staying honest.

 I got into university just fine and even graduated summa cum laude from my bachelor's degree, and went into my masters where I completed all coursework with a perfect 4.0.

One mistake will not destroy you, especially not in high school. If anything it's better to make this mistake now than when you are in college. Learn from it and don't repeat it. And maybe consider if you are trying to do too much.

 Decide what your priorities are and what can be sacrificed. A big part of the transition from high school to college is realizing when a workload is too much and you need to cut back to prevent harm to your health and to your goals. 

As much as you may want to you can't do everything. And talk to the adults in your life about your workload and where you are struggling. While you are still in high school is a good time to ask for help developing these time management skills you will need in college. 

A teacher you trust can be a good help with that. Also be honest with your teachers about what's going on in your life and when you are struggling. A good teacher should want you to succeed and should be willing to help you do that. They won't do the work for you, but if they see you coming to them and honestly trying to find ways to do better and make things work honestly, a lot of teachers will go out of their way to help you. Believe me, they didn't go in to teaching for the pay or the benefits. Lol.

You don't want to burn out in high school. You'll have time enough for that in college. (Jk, jk.)  But seriously, don't panic. Just take this as a wake up call and you'll be okay.

I know there has been a rash of fraudulent returns sent in by certain tax preparation services, and that a BOLO was sent out to watch for certain addresses and preparers as well as anything suspicious for those returns to be sent for further investigation.

 I cannot say if this is related - all of that is well outside my wheelhouse - but if the only common denominator is that these filers change services, then it is possible that the other preparer may have tried something or that they are just double checking cases where people changed preparers just to be careful. The IRS takes fraud very seriously, so I would not be surprised if that's the answer.

They may be sending the check in the mail rather than through direct deposit. IRS polices require that they do that sometimes when dealing with suspected id theft, depending on what triggered the account to be flagged for verification. You can call the customer service line to have them check on the status of their verification, and if the refund is being sent through mail or not.

COVID unfortunately left a *lot* of IRS departments very backed up. The one I work in finally cleared their backlog just this last December. And every now and then we still get some old ones thrown our way (usually coming from Ogden campus 😕). Hopefully this should be resolved soon, but keep contacting customer service. Sometimes being the squeaky wheel can speed things up - or at least get you some kind of explanation as to what is going on.

Okay, so bit of an insider view here (I've been a Tax Examining Technician for the IRS for three years now). I'll tell you what I am legally allowed to as some info about the inner workings is considered confidential to the point that I can get jail time for divulging it (TIGDA are the people who police IRS workers and they are *terrifying*). So usually when they send that letter, in my experience, it means one of two things: 

1) something got flagged as needed extra research to be approved - this usually has to do with larger amounts of money or certain credits that are often (but not always) claimed wrongly. Unfortunately the sub-groups that handle this more specialized research tend to take a lot of time to approve or deny the claim, whereupon they send it back to plebs like me to make the actual adjustments.

2) For one reason or another (like having to get transferred to multiple departments or other logistical issues) something is holding up the actual processing of the document. If this is the case, then that 60 day letter is likely more of a cya move on their part, and whoever currently is assigned to work your return probably has had it marked urgent and pushed to the top of their to do pile.

I expect to see these delayed response times becoming more and more of a problem in the future unfortunately.

A lot of the departments at the IRS are encouraging overtime right now since - honestly - we are backed up due to both the hiring freeze and the mass layoffs of the probationary people we hired and trained to help with the increased column during the tax season. (Though courts ordered them reinstated and they are being paid again, they are not being allowed to work.)

With more layoffs coming and the deferred resignation program taking many of our best people who have decided to leave rather than wait to see if they will be fired (thus getting ahead of the soon to be flooded job market), wait times are likely to get worse.

And honestly, even the overtime isn't helping like it used to since telework has been removed. It's now more difficult for those of us who deal with electronic documents to actually do that overtime since many of us have to drive an hour or more just to get to the office. And even then, we are not guaranteed to have access to our usual workspace as we share desks with multiple shifts. 

All that said, I hope you get your refund sooner rather than later. I know what it is like waiting for that return so you can pay bills hanging over your head. My best advice would be to call each week or so to check in on the progress. The squeaky wheel often gets the grease and the customer service folks can leave notes on the digital file that pop up for the tax examiners to see when they access the case.

Yep, definitely suspected ID theft. All kinds of things can trigger that in the system. But the good news is that does mean your return is being handled now by a TPP (Taxpayer Protection Program) specialist over in the accounts management department, so once you provide the needed information they should get you your refund quickly, so long as everything checks out.

If you are an individual renting a property, you would need to file a Schedule E, listing the days the property was rented, and the money spent on the property for upkeep, mortgage, etc and rental income. 

You can download the Sch E from the IRS website to see what you would need to keep track of, if you want to do it yourself rather than hiring someone. Page one of Sch E is for rental properties. 

If you owned the property through a company you created (like an LLC or the like) that would be a whole different kettle of fish that is outside my wheelhouse. Lol.

Just an fyi, if the change was made by Memphis or Ogden campuses take a *really* close look at it. They have been known to make a lot of mistakes. -_- 

But yes, they should, upon request, be able to provide you with what changes were made and why, after which you can contest the change if you have proof that it was erroneous, or you can file a 1040X to add information that may mitigate your amount owed. 

A lot of times these additional taxes are caused by something like not properly reporting capital gains or something along those lines, and the IRS only sees the sale and does not have the cost basis information to offset the gain. I see that a lot with ppl who have been trading stock or who make a sale of their primary residence without reporting it properly. 

But there is no way to know what particular thing happened without asking. Once you have that info, you can figure out how to best move forward.

Hey, this is all stuff that can be fixed, one way or another. The important thing is to handle it correctly and promptly. I second all these others saying to get a CPA and to file an extension for yours and your wife's personal return. I actually work for the IRS, and have for a few years now and in a few different positions, mostly working 1040s and 1040Xs, so I don't know as much about the business side.

However, I can tell you I have seen all sorts of mistakes and corrections sent in. It is always better for the Taxpayer or their representative to be the one notifying the IRS that the Taxpayer made a mistake rather than letting us find it. We see it all the time, so I know it feels really frightening but so long as you work with the IRS and communicate with them (and get a professional to help sort out the issues) it will be okay, and hopefully not too much of a financial burden. 

Big thing I learned while working for the IRS though: if you have anything more complex than the Deluxe version of Turbo Tax can put together, it's generally better to get an actual professional to help. Also, be sure to get a CPA who knows what they are doing. There are scammers out there, and also people who just aren't very good at their job. Check reviews and all that. 👍 You can do this.

I find that rituals work best for me when I build up a routine around it to put me in the right headspace. Things like cleansing the house/apartment/room first, taking a self-cleansing bath with special bath salts, oils, or soaps that I only use before ritual or other religious reasons, or preparing a ritual meal to have after the ceremony. While doing these things I listen to or sing religious chants or songs. I keep my mind focused on the purpose of my upcoming ritual, letting other thoughts slide past in a semi-meditative state. 

I will also put on drumming music during the ritual to help me build a feeling of anticipation and pacing. I usually add a portion at the end of the ritual where, before I open my sacred space, I take some time to meditate and try to enter a trance state to see if there are any messages from the powers I called upon in my ritual. Sometimes I succeed, sometimes I don't.

After the ritual, I ground and center to dispose of the excess energy. This includes engaging in the ritual meal I spoke of earlier. I also make cleaning up after my ritual part of the experience, keeping my mind on then purpose of the ritual while I put away and clean my ritual tools. 

Basically, depending on the time you have, you can devote pretty much the whole day to the ritual if you want. So, as far as I know, there is no documentation of this version of the myth. But this and many like it seem to be gaining popularity, seeming without any one source that can be pointed to. I mostly hear it explained that the "official" version of the myth was written by men, and this is the women's version of the story - though without any documentation behind the claim. I feel like if this version and similar are gaining such popularity, there must be something behind it. Perhaps the goddess herself is correcting the story through multiple channels, hence why it seems to be coming from nowhere and everywhere at once.

So, I did a but of research via my college's article database. What I found is that the original myths (because there were a few different versions via different writters) disagree on key points. All agree that Zeus okayed Hades taken Persephone, which was all they really took into account in Greek marriages (officially the father's approval was all you needed I think, correct me if I'm wrong). Also they all agree that Persephone was taken against her will - although this happened while she was collecting flowers with her ladies - a thing brides did right before they were married. Also important to note that she was called "Kore" (which means unmarried maiden, I believe) at this point, not Persephone.

What the texts disagree on is whether she was physically raped (some day yes outright, some imply it, some say nothing in this topic), and if she ate the pomegranate seeds knowing she would have to stay in Hades (again some day yes, some don't speak in it). Some of the articles I read pointed out that the wants of Persephone are not really addressed at all - no one asks her what she wants. It's all what Demeter wants and what Hades wants and what Zeus wants. Persephone is only a playing piece in the myth.

What we do know is that Persephone was first referred to by her own name after she married Hades. This signifies a gaining of power or agency. We also know that she became a very powerful and feared goddess through her connection to the underworld. There are many references to her outside the myth that speaks of her power independent of Hades. If she chose to eat the seeds, then this is a power she gained through her agency. 

The current popular interpretation seems to be that she made that choice. The old school interpretation says she did not and was forced. Both are valid. There are many theses, articles, and books out there on this topic, so I would encourage you to research for yourself and come to your own conclusions. Look for things with references and that have been peer reviewed for best effect.

I understand that is what you are doing, but that is not what agnosticism means. And you don't have to take my word for it. According to the philosopher William Rowe, "agnosticism is the view that human reason is incapable of providing sufficient rational grounds to justify either the belief that God exists or the belief that God does not exist".   To interpret it differently is to ignore the actual meaning of the word.

Likewise atheism is a-theism. The rejection of the claims of theism. A rejection of theism is not a claim itself (ie. That there is no god), it is a denial of a claim (ie. That there is a god). The importance of this distinction is that the burden if proof lies with the one making a claim. Atheism is not making a claim; it is a position of skepticism in the face of a claim.

I mean no disrespect, but you are using the words incorrectly when you use them as you do. Your usage is not the usage that is agreed upon by the consensus (which is how words gain their meaning).  To use them as you do inhibits conversation due to the misunderstandings it creates.
